## Highlights

- ARDL bounds test confirms cointegration between climate and agricultural value added in Türkiye (F = 8.706\*\*\*)
- Precipitation is the dominant climatic driver: +0.527% AVA increase per 1% precipitation rise (p < 0.10)
- Agricultural capital formation is the primary non-climatic driver: long-run conditional coefficient +0.375\*\*\* (p < 0.01); bidirectional causality (Toda–Yamamoto) precludes a structural-elasticity reading
- Land extensification is associated with declining productivity: long-run coefficient −2.349\*\*\* — consistent with expansion onto marginal land
- Temperature and CO₂ are nationally attenuated, consistent with spatial aggregation bias in semi-arid economies

---

## Abstract

This paper examines the long-run relationship between climate variability and agricultural value added (AVA) in Türkiye using annual data from 1970 to 2021 (T = 52). We apply the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds testing approach of @pesaran2001bounds, which accommodates the mixed integration order documented for the data: annual precipitation is I(0) while all other variables are I(1), precluding standard I(1)-based cointegration tests. The bounds F-statistic of 8.706 rejects the null of no cointegration at the 1 percent level. Three long-run coefficients are quantitatively important. Precipitation has an elasticity of +0.527 (p < 0.10), consistent with hydrological dominance in a semi-arid agrarian economy. Agricultural gross fixed capital formation has a long-run conditional coefficient of +0.375 (p < 0.01), in line with the Solow capital-deepening hypothesis, though a Toda–Yamamoto test detects bidirectional causality, so this coefficient is interpreted as a long-run cointegrating association rather than a structural productivity elasticity. Agricultural land area has a long-run association of −2.349 (p < 0.001), which we read as evidence of extensification onto ecologically marginal land accompanied by the ongoing structural shift toward higher-value horticulture on the shrinking land base. The temperature coefficient is insignificant at the national aggregate level, attributable to spatial aggregation across Türkiye's four bioclimatic zones, adaptation buffering, and variety switching. The per-capita CO₂ coefficient is likewise insignificant, consistent with the co-movement of this broad development-linked series with the dominant climatic and capital regressors in the sample. The error correction coefficient of −0.277 (p < 0.001) implies a disequilibrium half-life of 2.14 years (95% CI: 1.3–4.3 years). Results are robust across three specification checks, a semi-log temperature-anomaly re-estimation, and wild-bootstrap inference. Under IPCC mid-range projections of 10 percent precipitation reduction in the eastern Mediterranean by mid-century, the precipitation elasticity implies a long-run agricultural productivity loss of approximately USD 3.4 billion — the demand-side benchmark for evaluating irrigation investment. Policy implications centre on irrigation investment, green capital allocation, land consolidation, and sub-national data infrastructure.

**Keywords:** Climate change; Agricultural value added; ARDL bounds test; Türkiye; Land-use change; Precipitation elasticity; Capital formation

**JEL Classification:** Q54; Q12; C22; O13; Q15

## 1. Introduction

The relationship between climate variability and agricultural productivity constitutes one of the most policy-urgent empirical questions in development economics. For semi-arid middle-income economies — where rain-fed agriculture dominates production, irrigation coverage is structurally incomplete, and climate change projections point to sustained precipitation deficits and temperature increases well above the global average — quantifying the historical sensitivity of agricultural value added to climate fluctuations is a prerequisite for evidence-based adaptation policy.

This paper asks a concrete question: what is the long-run precipitation elasticity of agricultural value added in Türkiye, is it large enough to convert IPCC-projected rainfall deficits into quantifiable output losses, and does it remain stable once agricultural capital and land extensification are controlled for? Türkiye is a paradigmatic case: a major agricultural producer spanning four bioclimatic zones, with agricultural employment of 17.5 percent as of 2021, a 2053 net-zero target ratified in the Paris Agreement in October 2021, and an emerging domestic Carbon Law (Law No. 7547, 2025) that will reshape the incentive environment for agricultural production. Türkiye's agrarian structure carries deep institutional roots: the late Ottoman reforms of 1876–1908 restructured land tenure, regional crop diversification, and rural infrastructure across Anatolia in ways that shaped the spatial distribution of cultivated land, irrigation access, and farming practices whose long-run consequences this study empirically traces [@quataert2008]. Under IPCC [@ipcc2022wgii] mid-range scenarios, the eastern Mediterranean — including Türkiye — faces precipitation reductions of 5–15 percent and temperature increases of 1.5–3.5°C by mid-century, with agricultural productivity losses potentially exceeding 10–25 percent of current output in the most exposed regions [@giorgi2008climate].

The econometric literature on the climate–agricultural value added nexus in Türkiye has nevertheless remained sparse and methodologically incomplete. Existing studies either rely on crop-level agronomic and simulation approaches that cannot identify the aggregate historical relationship [@ozdog2011modeling; @demirdogen2024impact] or apply cointegration frameworks to narrower output concepts — agricultural production indices and sectoral CO$_2$ emissions — on shorter or crop-specific samples [@dumrul2017economic; @yurtkuran2021effect]. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study applies the ARDL bounds test methodology to the full climate–AVA nexus for Türkiye over a half-century horizon with the joint treatment of precipitation, temperature, capital formation, cultivated land, and per-capita emissions reported here.

This paper addresses that gap. The ARDL bounds test accommodates regressors of mixed integration order [@pesaran2001bounds], which matches our data: unit-root tests identify annual precipitation as I(0) while all other variables are I(1). This integration structure invalidates standard I(1)-based cointegration tests and has been documented for precipitation in the broader climate–agriculture literature [@dell2014weather; @chandio2020shortlong] but has not been addressed in any Turkish study. Our contribution is twofold. We establish the mixed-integration finding for Turkish climate–agricultural data, and we estimate long-run elasticities over a half-century sample using the ARDL framework with a joint five-variable treatment of precipitation, temperature, agricultural capital formation, cultivated land, and per-capita emissions. The resulting coefficients are directly interpretable and inform climate-adaptation policy design in semi-arid emerging economies.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the related literature. Section 3 presents the data and variable definitions. Section 4 describes the ARDL methodology. Section 5 reports the empirical results. Section 6 discusses policy implications and concludes.

---

## 2. Related Literature

The empirical literature on climate–agriculture linkages has developed rapidly over the past two decades, driven by methodological innovation and by the growing urgency of climate adaptation. Three strands are directly relevant to the present study.

The first strand comprises reduced-form cross-sectional and panel studies that exploit spatial and temporal variation in climate to identify productivity effects. @dell2012temperature demonstrate that temperature reduces GDP growth in poor countries, with agricultural income shocks as the primary transmission channel. @schlenker2009nonlinear establish nonlinear threshold effects of temperature on US crop yields using within-county panel variation. @lobell2007global estimate global-scale sensitivities of major crops to climate trends over 1961–2002. @ortiz-bobea2021 provide compelling cross-country evidence that human-caused climate change has already reduced agricultural total factor productivity by approximately 21 percent relative to a counterfactual without warming. These studies collectively establish the dominance of the hydrological channel and the ambiguity of temperature effects at aggregate spatial scales.

The second strand applies time-series methods — including the ARDL bounds test — to country-specific climate–agriculture data. @chandio2020shortlong apply ARDL to China, confirming positive precipitation and capital elasticities and insignificant temperature effects — a pattern closely paralleling our Turkish results. @ghosh2023climate deliver complementary ARDL and ECM evidence for Bangladesh, confirming a positive long-run precipitation elasticity and a statistically muted aggregate temperature response, with error correction operating at approximately one third per year. @janjua2010impact, for Pakistan, document a positive long-run rainfall effect and error correction at a rate of approximately 31 percent per year. @akinlo2014impact confirm cointegration between precipitation and agricultural GDP in Nigeria. @salami2009integrated document comparable patterns for Iran. The convergence of findings across these semi-arid and monsoonal agrarian economies suggests that precipitation dominance and temperature attenuation are systematic features of the climate–agriculture relationship in this development context. A parallel methodological trend within this strand has moved beyond CO$_2$ emissions to alternative environmental outcomes: @rahman2025epc apply CS-ARDL in a European panel to estimate the environmental Phillips curve using the load capacity factor as the dependent variable, demonstrating that the choice of environmental proxy materially shapes inference about growth–environment dynamics. Our use of agricultural value added as the outcome variable represents an analogous step in the climate-economy literature, capturing productive capacity directly rather than through an emissions intermediate.

The third strand focuses specifically on Türkiye and the MENA region. Turkish climate–agriculture research is dominated by crop-level and observational climatological work [@ozdog2011modeling; @demirdogen2024impact; @sensoy2007observed] that, while valuable, cannot identify the aggregate historical relationship between climate and agricultural value added. The small econometric literature combines short-sample ARDL exercises on an agricultural production index [@dumrul2017economic] with ARDL analyses of the agriculture–renewable-energy–CO$_2$ nexus that treat sectoral emissions rather than value added as the outcome [@yurtkuran2021effect; @pata2021linking]. These contributions establish basic short-run dynamics but do not address the mixed integration order of the underlying climate series, nor do they deliver long-run elasticities of agricultural value added over a half-century horizon. The present paper is, to our knowledge, the first to address these methodological gaps simultaneously for Türkiye: correct integration-order treatment, ARDL bounds testing on the full 1970–2021 sample, and comprehensive robustness validation.

## 3. Data and Variables

The analysis employs annual data for Türkiye over 1970–2021 (T = 52). The dependent variable is the log of agricultural value added at constant 2015 USD (ln AVA, units: USD), sourced from the World Bank World Development Indicators (WB WDI, series NV.AGR.TOTL.KD). Climate regressors are national average annual precipitation in millimetres (ln PR, units: mm yr⁻¹) and national average annual surface temperature in degrees Celsius (ln TSA, units: °C), both derived from the World Bank Climate Change Knowledge Portal (CCKP) by converting monthly series to annual arithmetic means. Additional regressors are agricultural gross fixed capital formation in constant 2015 USD (ln TSSO, units: USD, from FAOSTAT series Investment/Agriculture, forestry, fishing), agricultural land area in km² converted to 10³ ha (ln ALAN, units: 10³ ha, from WB WDI series AG.LND.AGRI.K2), and per-capita CO₂ emissions in metric tons per capita (ln CO₂, units: t CO₂ cap⁻¹, primary series WB WDI EN.ATM.CO2E.PC; the wild-bootstrap robustness environment in §5 substitutes the updated AR5-based series EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5 to assess data-vintage sensitivity). The choice to retain the legacy SAR-based series as primary while using the AR5-based series as robustness environment is deliberate: the primary estimation was frozen before the World Bank retired the legacy indicator, and a full re-estimation on the updated AR5 series yields F = 6.124 with qualitatively identical long-run signs and significance (see §5.1 footnote), so fixing the primary specification on the longer-established data vintage is the more conservative of the two admissible choices. Reporting both environments allows readers to assess sensitivity to the SAR-to-AR5 GWP transition directly rather than inferring it. The land area variable is divided by ten before log-transformation to convert from km² (WB native unit) to 10³ ha — since $1\,\text{km}^2 = 0.1\times 10^3\,\text{ha}$ — ensuring interpretability as a log-log elasticity. The per-capita CO₂ variable captures Türkiye's broader industrial-development pressure on the agricultural sector, normalised to population size; it is included to test whether rising per-capita carbon intensity is associated with agricultural productivity in the long run. All variables are expressed in natural logarithms, so all estimated coefficients are directly interpretable as elasticities. The sample is constrained to 1970–2021 by the latest available observation for the land area variable.

Table 1 provides descriptive statistics and unit root test results.

The descriptive statistics in Table 1 reveal three features that bear directly on the empirical strategy adopted in §4 and §5. First, the variation in ln AVA is moderate (S.D. = 0.42 around a mean of 24.83), reflecting steady but volatile real growth in the Turkish agricultural sector over the half-century covered. Second, the climate regressors exhibit very narrow ranges — ln PR varies between 6.09 and 6.67, and ln TSA between 2.40 and 2.65 — which is consistent with the quasi-stationary character of national climate aggregates and provides the empirical motivation for treating annual precipitation as I(0) under the bounds-testing framework. Third, the unit-root battery yields a clear and internally consistent classification: ADF, KPSS, and DF-GLS jointly support I(1) for ln AVA, ln TSA, ln TSSO, ln ALAN, and ln CO₂, while only ln PR is unambiguously I(0). This mixed-integration pattern explicitly violates the assumptions of @engle1987cointegration and @johansen1988statistical procedures and motivates the ARDL bounds approach that follows.

## 4. Methodology: ARDL Bounds Testing

The ARDL bounds test [@pesaran2001bounds] is the appropriate methodology when the variable set contains a mixture of I(0) and I(1) series, as confirmed by the unit root results in Table 1. Standard @engle1987cointegration and @johansen1988statistical cointegration tests assume all variables are I(1) — an assumption violated by the I(0) characterisation of annual precipitation. The ARDL framework is also robust to small samples [@narayan2005saving], making it well suited to the T = 52 annual time series available for Türkiye.

The I(0) classification of ln PR rests on three convergent pieces of evidence. The ADF test rejects the unit root null (stat = −4.127, p < 0.01) under a constant-only specification. The KPSS test fails to reject the null of stationarity (stat = 0.237, below the 10% critical value of 0.347), providing direct confirmation. The DF-GLS test yields marginal rejection at the 10% level (stat = −1.891), consistent with near-unit-root behaviour. The Zivot–Andrews test — which explicitly allows for a structural break near the 1988 Anatolian drought event (break year: 1988, stat = −4.698) — does not cross the 5% critical value (−4.80), suggesting the possibility of break-driven nonstationarity; however, since ADF and KPSS confirm stationarity without conditioning on a break, the preponderance of evidence supports the I(0) classification. The bounds F-test validity is unaffected regardless of whether ln PR is I(0) or I(1) [@pesaran2001bounds], so this classification question is consequential for motivation but not for inference.

The conditional error correction model (CECM) takes the form:

$$\Delta \ln \text{AVA}_t = \alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \alpha_i \Delta \ln \text{AVA}_{t-i} + \sum_{k} \sum_{j} \beta_{kj} \Delta X_{k,t-j} + \delta_1 \ln \text{AVA}_{t-1} + \sum_{k} \delta_k X_{k,t-1} + \varepsilon_t$$

where $X = \{\ln PR, \ln TSA, \ln TSSO, \ln ALAN, \ln CO_2\}$ and $\varepsilon_t$ is a white noise error. The optimal lag structure ARDL(4,0,1,0,2,0) is selected by the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) from a maximum of four lags per variable; the Schwarz Bayesian Criterion (SBC) selects a more parsimonious ARDL(1,0,0,0,1,0) that yields qualitatively identical long-run signs and significance but delivers a marginal bounds F-statistic (4.812, between the Narayan (2005) small-sample 5% upper bound of 4.26 and the 1% upper bound of 5.03) and exhibits residual serial correlation (BG LM(2) p = 0.031). We therefore follow @pesaran2001bounds in adopting the AIC specification, which produces a diagnostically clean residual process; robustness to the SBC structure is reported in the Online Appendix. The bounds F-test evaluates the joint null $H_0: \delta_1 = \delta_k = 0$ for all $k$ (no long-run relationship). If the F-statistic exceeds the upper I(1) bound of @pesaran2001bounds, cointegration is confirmed regardless of the actual integration order of the regressors. Long-run elasticities are recovered as $\theta_k = -\delta_k/\delta_1$; the error correction coefficient is $\delta_1$, expected to be negative and significant. Estimation uses the R `ARDL``ARDL` package [@natsiopoulos2022ardl], with bounds-test critical values from the Pesaran–Shin–Smith (2001) and Narayan (2005) critical-value tables.

## 5. Empirical Results

### 5.1. Cointegration Test

The bounds F-statistic of 8.706 (Table 2, Panel A) substantially exceeds the @pesaran2001bounds upper I(1) critical bound of 4.68 and the @narayan2005saving small-sample bound of 5.03, both at the 1 percent level for k = 5 regressors. The null of no long-run relationship is unambiguously rejected. This result establishes the statistical foundations for interpreting the long-run elasticities as genuine equilibrium relationships.^[An independent replication using the R `ARDL``ARDL` package [@natsiopoulos2022ardl] with the updated WB AR5 indicator (EN.GHG.CO2.PC.CE.AR5) and the nominal TSSO series yields F = 6.124, which also exceeds the 1% upper bound (4.68) and the Narayan (2005) bound (5.03), confirming cointegration under both data environments. The difference in F-statistics reflects the updated AR5 GWP methodology applied to the CO₂ series and the deflator applied to agricultural support expenditure; the primary estimates reported throughout the paper use the data vintage described in Table 1 (§3).]

The three panels of Table 2 jointly support the empirical-equilibrium interpretation that motivates the long-run analysis in §5.2 and the short-run dynamics in §5.3. Panel A confirms cointegration at the 1 percent level (F = 8.706, well above the @pesaran2001bounds I(1) bound of 4.68 and the @narayan2005saving small-sample bound of 5.03). Panel B reports five long-run coefficients of which three — precipitation, agricultural capital formation, and agricultural land — are statistically significant; their wild-bootstrap 95 percent confidence intervals all enclose the OLS point estimates, demonstrating that the inferential conclusions survive non-Gaussian residual structures and the SAR-to-AR5 data-vintage transition. Panel C confirms a negative and significant error-correction coefficient (−0.277, p < 0.001) and a passing diagnostic battery — no serial correlation, correct functional form, normality of residuals, homoskedasticity, and parameter stability over the full sample. Each of the long-run coefficients is interpreted in turn in §5.2; the short-run dynamics implied by the same CECM are reported in §5.3.

### 5.2. Long-Run Cointegrating Coefficients

**Precipitation (+0.527\*):** The positive and statistically significant long-run precipitation elasticity confirms the hydrological channel as the primary climatic determinant of Turkish agricultural productivity. A sustained 1 percent increase in national average annual precipitation raises agricultural value added by approximately 0.53 percent in long-run equilibrium — equivalent to approximately USD 258 million at 2021 price levels. This finding replicates the precipitation-dominance result of @chandio2020shortlong for China and @akinlo2014impact for Nigeria, suggesting that the hydrological channel systematically dominates in semi-arid agrarian economies with limited irrigation coverage. A second-order conditional-identification concern, that the precipitation coefficient is identified only conditional on the capital and land controls (both of which are themselves co-determined with agricultural value added), is empirically bounded by the Table 4 Panel (R2) robustness exercise: dropping lnALAN from the specification moves the precipitation coefficient from +0.527 to +0.598, a 13.5 percent change that lies well inside the band of reduced-form conditioning drift and indicates that the capital/land conditioning is not absorbing a material share of the precipitation signal.

**Capital formation (+0.375\*\*\*):** Agricultural gross fixed capital formation is the most precisely estimated determinant of long-run productivity. The long-run conditional coefficient is consistent with the @solow1956contribution capital-deepening hypothesis and implies that capital accumulation at the observed average rate of 3.2 percent per year is associated with approximately 1.2 percentage points per year of long-run agricultural value added growth over 1970–2021 — a descriptive co-movement rather than a causal structural elasticity.[^ty] This finding directly supports the policy case for redirecting agricultural support from production-linked transfers toward capital investment in irrigation infrastructure, mechanisation, and precision agriculture.

[^ty]: A bivariate Toda–Yamamoto test [@toda1995statistical] (augmented VAR with $k = 2$ lags selected by the Schwarz criterion plus $d_{\max} = 1$, yielding VAR(3)) rejects the null that lnAVA does not Granger-cause lnTSSO ($\chi^{2}(2) = 323.4$, $p < 0.001$), confirming bidirectional long-run causality consistent with counter-cyclical expansion of public agricultural support in response to sector output shocks. The +0.375 long-run coefficient is therefore interpreted as a conditional long-run association rather than a unidirectional structural productivity elasticity; instrumental-variable identification using DSI irrigation disbursements or EU pre-accession subsidy cycles would be required to recover the structural channel. The underlying VAR(3) passes the standard residual diagnostic battery (Ljung–Box Q(8) = 29.4, $p$ = 0.248; multivariate Jarque–Bera $p$ = 0.529; companion-matrix max $|\lambda| = 0.871 < 1$) and a wild-bootstrap ($B = 2000$, Rademacher $\pm 1$) re-computation of the Wald statistic yields a bootstrap median of 315.8 with a 95 percent CI of [282.1, 349.6], confirming that the large magnitude is not an artefact of residual misspecification but is consistent with the @dolado1996making simulation evidence that Wald statistics in strongly cointegrated augmented VARs can substantially exceed their asymptotic expectation in finite samples (full diagnostics in Online Appendix A5.3).

**Land area (−2.349\*\*\*):** The large, negative, and highly significant land area elasticity is the most counterintuitive finding and requires careful interpretation. It does not imply a negative marginal product of land per se. Rather, two complementary mechanisms are consistent with the observed pattern. First, over the sample period, Türkiye's total agricultural land area declined from roughly 28 million hectares in the early 1970s to approximately 23 million hectares by 2021 [@faostat2024landuse; @wb_ag_land_k2] — a contraction driven primarily by the abandonment of rain-fed cereal cultivation on marginal semi-arid plots and by conversion of low-productivity dryland to urban and infrastructural uses. The agricultural sector simultaneously shifted toward higher-value irrigated horticulture, viticulture, and orchards on the remaining land base. In this structural transformation context, the coefficient measures a conditional association in which falling total land area co-occurs with rising average value added per hectare, without implying a causal productivity-destruction effect. Second, to the extent that extensification episodes within the sample (e.g., the 1980s post-liberalisation cereal area expansion into Anatolian rangeland) brought lower-quality land into cultivation, the average product of the aggregate land endowment fell, generating the negative association in the time series. The long-run coefficient of −2.349 should therefore be read as a conditional association between the aggregate land area series and AVA in the presence of ongoing structural transformation, not as a production-function elasticity; structural identification using land-quality or irrigation-coverage instruments would be required to disentangle these channels. This caveat does not diminish the policy relevance: both mechanisms point toward consolidation and intensification as the appropriate pathway for Turkish agricultural development. Influence diagnostics computed on the ARDL long-run auxiliary regression of lnAVA on lnALAN (Cook's distance and DFBETA_{lnALAN}; full plots in Online Appendix A5) indicate that no single observation in the 1980–1988 post-liberalisation window exceeds the conventional influence thresholds ($D_i > 4/T$; $|\text{DFBETA}_i| > 2/\sqrt{T}$); the −2.349 estimate is therefore not an artefact of one or two leverage points but reflects the structural-transformation trajectory across the full half-century sample.

**Temperature and CO₂ (insignificant):** Neither the log of mean surface temperature nor per-capita CO₂ emissions are statistically significant in the long-run equation. The positive sign on the temperature coefficient (+0.184) deserves comment, since it runs counter to the negative partial-temperature effects documented for Mediterranean crops above approximately 25°C in the meta-analytic literature [@schlenker2009nonlinear; @hatfield2011climate]. Two mechanisms are consistent with a positive-but-insignificant estimate at the national level. First, Türkiye's annual mean temperature over the sample period ranges from 12.1°C to 14.2°C, a range that lies largely below the damage thresholds identified for wheat, maize, and sunflower — Türkiye's dominant crops — so warming may have extended growing seasons and shifted mean temperatures toward agronomically favourable ranges in the cooler highland interior. Second, spatial aggregation across Türkiye's four bioclimatic zones (Black Sea, Mediterranean, semi-arid Anatolian plateau, eastern continental) mixes regions where warming is beneficial against those where heat stress is damaging, attenuating both the sign and magnitude of the aggregate estimate. The semi-log robustness check using the mean-centred temperature anomaly confirms aggregate insignificance (θ = +0.059, p = 0.198; Appendix A4). We therefore attribute the aggregate null to spatial aggregation bias, adaptation buffering, variety switching, and CO₂ fertilisation–heat stress partial cancellation, rather than to genuine temperature insensitivity of Turkish agriculture. The per-capita normalisation of the CO₂ series further implies that the coefficient captures the agricultural response to Türkiye's broader development-linked emissions intensity rather than to sector-specific environmental pressure. **Omitted-trend falsification:** if rising per-capita CO₂ — which co-moves with industrialisation, urbanisation, and agricultural input intensification — were driving the long-run AVA trajectory as an omitted industrial-development trend, its coefficient should be negative and significant. The statistically neutral estimate (θ = +0.063, t = 0.335) falsifies this concern and supports the interpretation that the precipitation and capital coefficients are not proxying for Türkiye's secular industrialisation path. The same aggregate attenuation of temperature appears in ARDL analyses for Bangladesh [@ghosh2023climate], China [@chandio2020shortlong], and Iran [@salami2009integrated], and in the cross-country productivity evidence of @ortiz-bobea2021. At the crop or regional level, temperature effects remain important; the present result is about the limits of nationally aggregated annual data, not about temperature insensitivity per se.

Constant included but not reported. Short-run coefficients on capital formation (ΔlnTSSO) and land area (ΔlnALAN) are interpreted as predictive associations; the endogeneity caveat applying to the long-run cointegrating equation extends to the short-run dynamics.

The error correction coefficient of −0.277 (p < 0.001) implies that 27.7 percent of any disequilibrium between agricultural value added and its long-run determinants is corrected within one year, with a half-life of approximately 2.1 years. This adjustment speed is economically plausible given agricultural capital durability and multi-season crop cycles. Several features of the short-run dynamics deserve comment. First, the autoregressive structure of agricultural value added (ΔlnAVA lags 1–3: coefficients −0.604\*\*\*, −0.246\*\*, −0.236\*\*) indicates strong mean-reversion in growth rates — above-trend years are followed by below-trend years, consistent with production cycle dynamics, price corrections, and soil fatigue. Second, contemporaneous precipitation (ΔlnPR: +0.096\*\*\*) generates a statistically significant and precisely estimated positive short-run impact: a 1 percent current-year increase in national precipitation is associated with a 0.096 percent current-year increase in agricultural value added, a plausible magnitude given the dominance of rain-fed production. Third, the land area dynamics exhibit an interesting lag structure: contemporaneous area expansion is statistically insignificant (−0.298, p = 0.323), while the one-year lagged expansion generates a large and significant positive short-run effect (ΔlnALAN\_{t-1}: +1.075\*\*\*), consistent with the gestation period between land clearing and productive cultivation and with the short-run lag structures documented for comparable semi-arid agrarian economies [@chandio2020shortlong; @ghosh2023climate]. Fourth, short-run capital formation, temperature, and CO₂ shocks do not translate immediately into agricultural value added; their effects, where present, operate through the long-run level relationship rather than within-year dynamics.

### 5.4. Robustness

Three robustness checks confirm the stability of the core findings (Table 4). First, excluding CO₂ from the specification — to rule out multicollinearity with temperature — leaves the precipitation (+0.541\*) and capital (+0.388\*\*\*) elasticities largely unchanged and the temperature coefficient insignificant. Second, excluding land area leaves the precipitation (+0.598\*) and capital (+0.461\*\*\*) elasticities stable. Third, sub-sample estimation over 1980–2021 (raw T = 42, effective $T_{\text{eff}} = 38$ after lag truncation, post-liberalisation) confirms cointegration (F = 6.814\*\*\*) and yields qualitatively identical coefficient signs and significance patterns (ECT = −0.241\*\*\*, ln PR = +0.489\*, ln TSSO = +0.352\*\*\*, ln ALAN = −2.108\*\*\*). The CUSUM and CUSUM-of-Squares tests confirm structural parameter stability throughout the full sample.

**Functional-form considerations for temperature.** The log transformation of mean surface temperature has precedent in the reduced-form ARDL literature [@chandio2020shortlong; @ghosh2023climate], though the climate-econometrics literature more commonly uses levels (°C) or anomalies relative to a climatological baseline [@dell2014weather; @schlenker2009nonlinear]. Türkiye's annual mean temperature ranges from 12.1 °C to 14.2 °C over 1970–2021, with a coefficient of variation of about 2 percent ($\text{CV} \approx 0.02$). Over this narrow range, a log-log fit and a semi-log fit with temperature in levels are numerically close, so the log elasticity reported here is approximately equal to the semi-elasticity that would be obtained under the more standard level-temperature specification. A formal semi-log re-estimation using the mean-centred temperature anomaly (TSA$-\overline{\text{TSA}}$, °C) is reported in the Online Appendix (Appendix Table A4); the statistical insignificance of the aggregate temperature effect is confirmed (TSA anomaly coefficient = +0.059, p = 0.198), consistent with the spatial-aggregation and adaptation-buffering mechanisms discussed in §5.2. The Appendix A4 bounds F-statistic (5.323) remains above the @pesaran2001bounds 1 percent upper bound (4.68) and the @narayan2005saving small-sample bound (5.03), so the cointegration verdict itself — not merely the significant long-run coefficients — survives the semi-log functional-form transformation. The Appendix A4 precipitation point estimate (+0.227) remains positive and of a qualitatively similar magnitude to the primary log-log estimate (+0.527), although with a wider standard error that reduces it to formal insignificance at conventional levels. This efficiency loss is consistent with a larger Appendix A4 error-correction coefficient (−0.393 vs. primary −0.277) that shifts variance explanation toward faster short-run adjustment and away from the long-run precipitation coefficient, rather than with a substantive overturning of the hydrological-dominance conclusion.

The primary estimates reported here confirm ECT stability and are the basis for all inferences drawn in §5.4.

The robustness exercises summarised in Table 4 reinforce three claims that anchor the Discussion in §6. First, the bounds F-statistic remains well above the @pesaran2001bounds 1 percent upper bound across all three specifications (range: 6.81 to 7.84), so the cointegration verdict is not driven by any single regressor or sub-sample. Second, the precipitation, capital, and land coefficients retain their signs, magnitudes, and statistical significance — the precipitation elasticity moves within the band [+0.489, +0.598], the capital elasticity within [+0.352, +0.461], and the land coefficient within [−2.318, −2.108]. Third, the temperature and per-capita CO₂ coefficients remain statistically insignificant in every specification, consistent with the aggregate-attenuation interpretation advanced in §5.2. The error-correction term is negative and statistically significant throughout (−0.241 to −0.289), confirming the long-run equilibrium-restoration interpretation. The robustness battery validates the use of the baseline ARDL(4,0,1,0,2,0) estimates as the basis for the policy discussion that follows.

\newpage

## 6. Discussion, Policy Implications, and Conclusions

This paper delivers five empirical findings for the climate–agricultural value added nexus in Türkiye. First, a stable long-run cointegrating relationship exists (F = 8.706\*\*\*). Second, precipitation is the dominant climatic determinant, with an elasticity of +0.527 that provides a quantitative basis for cost-benefit analysis of irrigation investment: under the @giorgi2008climate mid-range projection of 10 percent precipitation reduction in the eastern Mediterranean by mid-century, the model predicts a long-run agricultural productivity loss of approximately USD 3.4 billion — providing the demand-side benchmark against which adaptation costs should be evaluated. Third, capital formation is the primary non-climatic productivity driver (+0.375\*\*\*), supporting the reorientation of agricultural support from consumption transfers toward green capital investment. Fourth, land extensification is productivity-reducing (−2.349\*\*\*), motivating land consolidation and marginal land retirement policies. Fifth, temperature and CO₂ are aggregate-attenuated — a finding transferable to comparable semi-arid emerging economies.

Four policy points follow. First, the precipitation elasticity provides a direct benchmark for evaluating the DSI (State Hydraulic Works) irrigation expansion programme: under coefficient uncertainty, a 10 percent rainfall shortfall maps into a long-run AVA loss of roughly USD 0.1 to 6.6 billion (95% CI derived from the asymptotic Delta-method SE; point estimate USD 3.4 billion, computed from a 2021 AVA base of approximately USD 64 billion at constant 2015 prices, WB WDI series NV.AGR.TOTL.KD), which is the demand-side benchmark against which adaptation costs should be evaluated. This benchmark is primarily actionable by DSİ (Devlet Su İşleri) in planning irrigation coverage expansion and by the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry (TAGEM) in climate-adaptation programme design; it is less immediately actionable by smallholder farmers or rain-fed cereal producers in low-irrigation provinces who lack access to supplemental irrigation infrastructure — a distributional gap that climate adaptation policy must explicitly address. Second, the long-run conditional capital-formation coefficient (+0.375\*\*\*) — interpreted as a cointegrating association rather than a structural productivity elasticity in light of the Toda–Yamamoto bidirectional-causality finding (§5.2 footnote 1) — supports reallocating agricultural support from production-linked transfers towards capital investment in irrigation infrastructure, mechanisation, and precision agriculture, which are currently underweighted in Türkiye's agricultural support architecture. This reallocation is within the authority of the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry through the Agricultural Support Framework (Tarımsal Destekleme Çerçevesi) and is conditional on budgetary flexibility within the constraints of the current medium-term fiscal programme; it would benefit primarily commercially oriented farms with access to formal credit, potentially widening the productivity gap between large irrigated and small rain-fed operations if not accompanied by targeted TKDK (IPARD) co-financing. Third, if the negative land-area coefficient (−2.349\*\*\*) reflects extensification onto marginal and hydrologically stressed terrain — as the Turkish LULUCF evidence in @ozdog2011modeling and related regional studies suggests — then policies promoting marginal-land retirement and consolidation over further extensification are warranted; this conclusion is conditional on confirming the extensification-onto-marginal-land mechanism via sub-national data, and the distributional cost falls disproportionately on smallholder households in dryland cereal regions whose livelihoods depend on extensive cultivation; this interpretation should be confirmed by a structural identification exercise before the policy conclusion is treated as fully robust. Fourth, the national-aggregate null on temperature should not be read as evidence of sub-national robustness; that question requires a provincial agricultural panel, which is not currently available for Türkiye at the needed resolution, and any provincial-level adaptation policy targeting heat-stressed regions (southeastern Anatolian plateau, Çukurova basin) should be informed by finer spatial data than the aggregate evidence presented here permits.

The methodological contribution — demonstrating that the I(0) character of precipitation invalidates I(1)-based cointegration methods and motivates the ARDL framework — provides a replicable template for applied researchers working with climate and agricultural time series in settings where this integration structure is common but rarely examined. Three limitations should be noted. Aggregate annual data impose spatial and temporal averaging that can mask sub-national heterogeneity. The linear specification rules out asymmetric responses to positive and negative precipitation shocks. Capital formation and cultivated land are endogenous in a reduced-form setting, and the non-climate coefficients should therefore be interpreted as long-run conditional associations rather than as structural elasticities. Natural extensions include an NARDL specification for asymmetric response [@shin2014modelling]; a @bai2003computation multiple structural break test to locate regime shifts around the 1980 liberalisation, the 2001 macroeconomic crisis, and the post-2008 agricultural support reform — noting that the small-sample supF distribution is a $\chi^{2}(q)$ approximation that should be cross-checked via a restricted bootstrap before inferential claims are drawn; a provincial panel with @dumitrescu2012testing causality; and instrumental variable estimation using DSI irrigation-programme disbursements as an instrument for agricultural capital. A final methodological caveat concerns the land coefficient: the two mechanisms advanced for the −2.349 estimate — structural transformation toward higher-value irrigated production and marginal-land extensification under declining aggregate quality — are observationally equivalent under the present reduced-form specification, since both predict the same negative sign on the aggregate land area series; future work with sub-national data could separate them by exploiting a Bartik-type shift-share instrument on provincial irrigation-coverage growth to isolate the structural-transformation channel from the marginal-land channel.

The AIC-selected ARDL(4,0,1,0,2,0) is reported as primary in §5; the HQ-selected intermediate specification and the parsimonious SBC-selected ARDL(1,0,0,0,1,0) are included to address the concern raised in the peer-review process that the SBC specification exhibits residual serial correlation at the 5 percent level.

*Note:* \*\*\* p < 0.01; \*\* p < 0.05; \* p < 0.10. All three specifications are estimated on the full 1970–2021 sample. The long-run coefficient signs and statistical significance are stable across the three information criteria; the error-correction speed of adjustment is stable in the range $[-0.342, -0.277]$. The SBC-selected parsimonious specification fails the Breusch–Godfrey LM(2) serial-correlation test at the 5 percent level (p = 0.031), consistent with the standard symptom of under-parameterisation: the ARDL(1,0,0,0,1,0) structure is too short to absorb the three-year autoregressive dynamics of lnAVA documented in §5.3 (ΔlnAVA$_{t-1}$, ΔlnAVA$_{t-2}$, ΔlnAVA$_{t-3}$ all statistically significant). The AIC- and HQ-selected specifications both pass the full diagnostic battery. We therefore adopt the AIC-selected ARDL(4,0,1,0,2,0) as primary throughout §5, following the diagnostic-clean selection principle of @pesaran2001bounds; the HQ-selected intermediate specification is available in the replication package and yields qualitatively identical inference.

**A5.2 Land-coefficient influence diagnostics.** Figure A5.1 plots Cook's distance $D_i$ and the studentised DFBETA for lnALAN from the long-run auxiliary regression of lnAVA on the five long-run regressors. Conventional influence thresholds are $D_i > 4/T \approx 0.077$ and $|\text{DFBETA}_i| > 2/\sqrt{T} \approx 0.277$ for $T = 52$. No observation in the 1980–1988 post-liberalisation window exceeds either threshold. The maximum Cook's distance across the full sample is $D_{\max} = 0.061$ (observed in 1985, below the threshold), and the maximum $|\text{DFBETA}_{\text{lnALAN}}|$ is 0.218 (observed in 1988, below the threshold). The −2.349 long-run land coefficient is therefore not driven by one or two leverage observations; it reflects the structural-transformation trajectory of Turkish agriculture across the full half-century sample. The raw influence-diagnostic series is archived in the Zenodo replication package (`A5_influence_diagnostics.csv``A5_influence_diagnostics.csv`).

**A5.3 Toda–Yamamoto augmented-VAR residual diagnostics and bootstrap-based Wald inference.** The bivariate Toda–Yamamoto test reported in the §5.2 footnote uses an augmented VAR($k + d_{\max}$) = VAR(3) in $(\ln\text{AVA}, \ln\text{TSSO})$, with lag order $k = 2$ selected by the Schwarz criterion and $d_{\max} = 1$ set equal to the maximum observed order of integration across the two series. The null of Granger non-causality is tested by a Wald restriction on the first $k = 2$ lag coefficients in each equation. The realised test statistic ($\chi^{2}(2) = 323.4$) is large relative to its asymptotic expectation of 2; Table A5.2 reports the residual diagnostics and a wild-bootstrap Wald replication that together confirm the statistic is not an artefact of residual misspecification.

**Table A5.2. Toda–Yamamoto VAR(3) Residual Diagnostics and Bootstrap-Based Wald Statistic**

| Diagnostic | Test statistic | p-value | Verdict |
|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Portmanteau (Ljung–Box multivariate, 8 lags) | Q(8) = 29.41 | 0.248 | No residual autocorrelation |
| Jarque–Bera multivariate normality | JB = 3.172 | 0.529 | Residuals jointly normal |
| VAR stability (max $|\lambda|$ of companion matrix) | 0.871 | — | Stable (all roots inside unit circle) |
| Asymptotic Wald ($\chi^{2}(2)$) | 323.4 | < 0.001 | Reject non-causality |
| Wild-bootstrap Wald (B = 2000, Rademacher ±1) | 315.8 (median) | < 0.001 | Reject non-causality |
| Bootstrap Wald 95% CI | [282.1, 349.6] | — | Excludes asymptotic critical value (5.99) by two orders of magnitude |

*Note:* Bootstrap implementation follows the recursive-residual scheme of @hacker2006tests with Rademacher ±1 weights, B = 2000 replications. The magnitude of the statistic, while large, is consistent with the simulation evidence of @dolado1996making that finite-sample Wald statistics in augmented VARs can substantially exceed their asymptotic expectation when the underlying bivariate process is strongly cointegrated, as here ($F_{\text{bounds}} = 8.706$, §5.1). The residual diagnostic battery — no autocorrelation, joint normality, and companion-matrix stability — rules out the two standard mechanisms that would have inflated the denominator of the Wald statistic (residual autocorrelation and variance under-estimation). The conclusion of bidirectional causality between lnAVA and lnTSSO is therefore not sensitive to the inferential framework.
